description:
Crewcial is a physician-led team advancing astronaut health and safer human spaceflight. 🚀

We’re seeking collaborators in software development, AI/ML, data science, visualization, and UI/UX to turn our ideas into practical solutions.

Join us! your expertise could be the missing piece!
summary: When Earth is 20 minutes away, Crewcial puts a physician's judgment on board. It is an offline web app that helps astronauts check their own health and know what to do next. In a 2-minute daily check-in, astronauts enter blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, sleep, mood, stress and symptoms. Two built-in tests add objective data: a reaction test modelled on NASA's Reaction Self Test, and an Amsler grid for vision changes. Crewcial compares each result with the astronaut's own in-flight normal, because Earth ranges can mislead in space. Each body system on an astronaut figure gets a status in colour, icon and word, with the next step and who to tell: self-care, the crew medical officer, or the flight surgeon through a private report. Advice adapts to a station, the Moon or Mars. Crewcial also catches the "blind spot": feeling alert while testing slower than usual. All 47 clinical rules are published standards or a cautious medical judgement by an aerospace physician, and every status shows the rule behind it. NASA made its first medical evacuation from the ISS in January 2026. From Mars, evacuation may not be possible, so the first check must happen on board. Prototype with simulated data; not a medical device.
details:
What it does

Crewcial helps astronauts on long missions check their own health and act on the result. After a short daily check-in, each body system shows one status, the next step and who to tell. It runs offline in any browser and keeps every reading on the device.

How it works

Check-in: blood pressure, resting heart rate, temperature, sleep, mood, stress and a symptom check by body system. Blood sugar and oxygen saturation are added when there is a reason.

Built-in tests: a 3-minute reaction test modelled on the PVT-B in NASA's Reaction Self Test, preceded by a 0–10 alertness rating, and an Amsler grid for each eye to catch vision changes linked to SANS.

Personal normal: after a learning period, each reading is compared with the astronaut's own range on this mission, not with an Earth table.

Statuses: Act now, Watch, Re-check, No data, Learning your normal, and In your range, each a colour, an icon and a word , following NASA-STD-3001 Vol. 2, Appendix F. Missing data is never green. Act-now limits and red-flag symptoms do not wait for a baseline; one unusual day asks for a re-check, and a lasting change becomes Watch. "Why this colour?" shows the rule, its source and its sign-off.

Combined patterns: fatigue, possible infection, vision change, and the blind spot, when an astronaut feels as alert as usual but tests slower.

Escalation: self-care, then the crew medical officer's checklist, then the flight surgeon through a private four-part report the astronaut approves. Urgent but non-emergency findings, such as 39.1 °C or blood sugar of 200 mg/dL or more, go to the CMO today, and safety-critical tasks wait for the flight surgeon. A spacewalk readiness summary lists open flags and never says go or no-go.

Settings: space station (real-time link), Moon (4–12 s one way) and Mars (up to 20 minutes one way, with a reply countdown). Learn cards answer the challenge's five questions for each indicator.

Clinical validity

All 47 rules come from a checked source (NEWS2, the 2025 AHA/ACC blood pressure guideline, ADA Standards of Care 2026, the PVT-B validation paper) or is a cautious medical judgement by an aerospace physician. The app lists 45 sources, from NASA's Human Research Program and NASA-STD-3001 to the Canadian Space Agency and JAXA.

Testing

89 of 89 rule and scenario tests and 222 of 222 browser checks pass. A shadow run on simulated data (20 crew, 180 days, 60 injected events: blood-pressure rises, fatigue, low mood and fever) flagged all 60 events (95% CI 94–100%), on average 0.65 days after onset; 5.9% of flagged days fell outside any event (95% CI 3.5–9.2%), just above our under-5% target: about one false alarm per 160 quiet crew-days. This checks the logic, not clinical accuracy.

Benefits and impact

The crew gets a structured first check on board when Earth is minutes away, and the flight surgeon gets earlier, clearer reports. Private-by-default data and crew-approved reports lower the fear of losing flight status, which drives under-reporting. As commercial spaceflight grows, a flight surgeon for every flyer is not feasible. On Earth, the same approach fits places where help is far away, such as Concordia station in the Antarctic winter, or locally in Makkah, during Hajj, as a phone app linked to a local emergency department.

What is creative

Each astronaut is their own reference. Objective tests sit beside self-report, and the app flags when feeling and performance disagree. Advice changes with distance from Earth, and every colour explains itself.

Factors considered

False reassurance (no data is never green), alarm fatigue (tiers, sustained changes, a learning period), typing errors (plausibility checks), privacy (mood is never shown to crewmates), over-reliance (advisory only; medication only as directed by the flight surgeon or protocol), crew time (a two-minute design target) and Mars delay (fully offline, with store-and-forward reports).

Tools

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks or outside libraries; charts and the astronaut figure are drawn in code, and the rules are kept as data. Tests use Node.js, and Playwright with Chrome. Hosting: GitHub Pages (https://sakhaahm.github.io/Crewcial/); the code is at https://github.com/SakhaaHM/Crewcial under the Apache-2.0 licence. The code was written with Claude (Anthropic) under my direction. No special hardware: it runs on a phone or laptop.

Who made it and what's next

Team Crewcial is my solo entry. I'm Dr. Sakhaa Almadani, an aerospace medicine physician. I want to bridge medicine and technology to protect human health in extreme environments, both in space and on Earth. Next: an analog mission with a communication delay, a short-mission mode based on preflight readings, and wearable sensors for autonomous, real-time readings.

Limits

A prototype with simulated data, not a medical device. The check-in has not yet been timed with users. A slow decline over weeks can go unflagged, because the personal range follows it; a separate check for that is future work.
